ai-at-work.title: Salesforce rolls out new Slackbot AI agent as it battles Microsoft and Google in workplace AI
ai-at-work.excerpt: Salesforce on Tuesday launched an entirely rebuilt version of Slackbot, the company's workplace assistant, transforming it from a simple notification tool into what executives describe as a fully powe
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Salesforce rebuilt Slackbot from a basic notification tool into a full AI agent that can search data, write documents, and execute tasks directly in Slack. This matters because workplace AI assistants are becoming the actual interface where work gets done, not just another notification channel gathering dust. The real test isn't whether Salesforce can build fancy AI, it's whether anyone will actually use it or if it becomes another chatbot graveyard collecting digital tumbleweeds.

ai-at-work.title: Anthropic launches Cowork, a Claude Desktop agent that works in your files — no coding required
ai-at-work.excerpt: Anthropic released Cowork on Monday, a new AI agent capability that extends the power of its wildly successful Claude Code tool to non-technical users — and according to company insiders, the team bui
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Anthropic released Cowork, an AI agent that lets non-technical users automate file-based tasks in Claude Desktop without writing code. This matters because digital workplace leaders are drowning in requests to integrate AI into actual workflows, and having tools that bypass the developer bottleneck could finally make that happen at scale. The fact that they built this in ten days using their own tool is either genuinely impressive or a masterclass in PR timing, depending on how well it actually works in the real world.

ai-at-work.title: Nous Research's NousCoder-14B is an open-source coding model landing right in the Claude Code moment
ai-at-work.excerpt: Nous Research, the open-source artificial intelligence startup backed by crypto venture firm Paradigm, released a new competitive programming model on Monday that it says matches or exceeds several la
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Nous Research just dropped NousCoder-14B, an open-source coding model that claims to match bigger proprietary systems while being trained in four days on 48 Nvidia chips. For digital workplace pros, this matters because it signals that capable coding assistance is becoming commodity infrastructure rather than a proprietary moat, which means your vendor lock-in days are numbered and your negotiating position just improved. The real story here isn't the model itself, it's that we're watching the AI coding assistant market tip from "expensive proprietary magic" to "pick your open alternative," and that's always when things get interesting for IT budgets.

ai-at-work.title: How AI stacks are rewriting the rules of business
ai-at-work.excerpt: The shift from on-premises computing to software as a service changed the technology model and forced information technology organizatios to modernize how it builds, buys and operates software. It als
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Companies are layering AI tools into their existing tech stacks and discovering it's forcing them to rethink how they buy, deploy, and operate software across the organization. This matters because your procurement process, vendor relationships, and internal governance structures are about to get messy if you haven't already started adapting. The real talk: most organizations are still trying to figure out how to expense AI tools, let alone integrate them sensibly into their workflows, so buckle up for a bumpy ride.

tools-tech.title: Microsoft says it’s making AI ‘safe for work’ in your browser
tools-tech.excerpt: Microsoft is testing the addition of agentic AI to its corporate browser, Edge for Business. A new version, currently available in a limited preview, will help perform routine tasks more efficiently,
tools-tech.dwp_take: Microsoft is rolling out agentic AI features in Edge for Business that can handle multi-step tasks like form filling and information gathering. This matters because your users will expect these kinds of AI helpers across all their tools, so you need to think now about governance, security, and whether your processes can actually handle automated workflows without creating chaos. Honestly, the real test isn't whether the AI works, it's whether your organization can handle the consequences when it doesn't.

tools-tech.title: Microsoft, EY to spend $1 billion on helping customers buy agentic AI
tools-tech.excerpt: Microsoft and EY will spend $1 billion on helping their customers adopt AI over the next five years. The billion will support assisting clients with pioneering AI projects and capability building, sai
tools-tech.dwp_take: Microsoft and EY are dropping a billion dollars to help their enterprise customers actually implement agentic AI over the next five years instead of just talking about it. This matters because digital workplace leaders are drowning in AI announcements but starving for real implementation guidance and resources. Honestly, it's refreshing when vendors put actual money behind adoption help rather than just selling licenses and hoping you figure it out yourself.

tools-tech.title: Workday extends Sana AI to ITSM after HR, finance
tools-tech.excerpt: Workday conversational AI platform Sana for Workday is now ready to talk about IT Service Management (ITSM) automation as part of the company’s broader effort to help enterprises streamline workflows,
tools-tech.dwp_take: Workday is expanding its Sana AI chatbot beyond HR and finance into IT Service Management, adding automation for employee onboarding, access changes, and routine IT requests. This matters because IT teams are drowning in repetitive tickets, so if Sana can actually handle these without creating more work for humans, that's a real win. The real test will be whether it reduces tickets or just becomes another tool people ignore in favor of calling the help desk anyway.

tools-tech.title: With AI, typing’s out, talking’s in
tools-tech.excerpt: Eight months ago, LinkedIn co-founder and former CEO Reid Hoffman confessed: “I am voicepilled.” He argued that talking instead of typing was the next great leap in computing. Being “voicepilled,” he
tools-tech.dwp_take: Voice interfaces are gaining serious traction as productivity tools, with influential tech leaders arguing that speaking is fundamentally faster and more natural than typing. Digital workplace pros need to start thinking about how voice-first workflows will reshape everything from documentation to collaboration, especially as AI gets better at understanding context and nuance. That said, calling the keyboard a "Victorian-era contraption" is pure Silicon Valley theater, because I've yet to meet a knowledge worker who wants their sensitive emails or code commits captured through office ambient sound.

digital-culture.title: Bosses take remote less work seriously when it’s geared toward parents, study shows
digital-culture.excerpt: Being penalized for using flexible working policies—remote work, hybrid work, parental leave, and more—can be subtle, or screamingly obvious. Nicole Yelland, a communications strategist from Detroit,
digital-culture.dwp_take: A new study confirms what many already knew: managers treat flexible work requests differently depending on the reason, with parental leave and family-focused remote work getting the short end of the stick compared to other flexibility requests. This matters because it directly impacts retention, productivity, and your legal exposure, since selective enforcement of flexible work policies creates discrimination claims waiting to happen. Here's the kicker: if your leadership team still thinks a sick kid at home is less legitimate than someone's "deep work focus day," you've got a culture problem that no Slack integration will fix.

digital-culture.title: AI is already killing the executive assistant job
digital-culture.excerpt: There is a growing body of evidence that AI is redefining white-collar work. It’s not just the endless rounds of layoffs at tech companies that herald this transformation. Entry-level jobs are disappe
digital-culture.dwp_take: AI tools are automating executive assistant tasks like scheduling, email management, and research, shrinking demand for entry-level roles that traditionally trained younger workers. This matters because executive assistant jobs have long been the on-ramp for people building corporate careers, and losing them means fewer pathways into organizations and fewer mentorship opportunities overall. The irony is that executives are now using AI to replace the very people who used to make their lives functional, which saves money but costs institutional knowledge and actually makes most executives worse at their jobs.

digital-culture.title: AI may be eating jobs, but it poses an even bigger threat
digital-culture.excerpt: The AI conversation today focuses on systems. Which jobs will survive? How does education need to adapt? What happens to the economy when machines produce what humans used to? Governments are commissi
digital-culture.dwp_take: Fast Company is arguing that while job displacement from AI gets all the attention, there's a bigger threat we're actually ignoring and could do something about. For digital workplace leaders, this means the real crisis isn't robots taking jobs, it's that we're spending energy on the wrong conversations while missing what we can actually control right now. Honestly, this reminds me of watching people argue about the Titanic's deck chairs while forgetting to ask what the actual iceberg problem is.

digital-culture.title: Managers are unprepared to lead a human-agent hybrid workforce
digital-culture.excerpt: Andrew Reece, Chief AI Scientist, BetterUp The introduction of AI agents into the corporate workforce is not like other technology disruptions. Unlike previous automation, agents are empowered to act
digital-culture.dwp_take: A new study confirms what many of us already suspected: most managers have no idea how to oversee teams where AI agents make autonomous decisions alongside humans. This matters because your workforce is about to become something your management training never prepared anyone for, and pretending the old playbook still works will tank productivity and employee trust. The real problem isn't the AI agents themselves, it's that we're asking managers trained to supervise spreadsheets to suddenly govern systems that think independently.

industry-news.title: This week in 5 numbers: More than 1 in 5 employees say they’ve witnessed unethical or illegal conduct at work
industry-news.excerpt: Here’s a roundup of numbers from the last week of HR news — including how many women hold seats on the corporate boards of Russell 3000 companies.
industry-news.dwp_take: More than one in five employees have witnessed unethical or illegal conduct at work, according to HR Dive's weekly numbers roundup. This matters because it tells you your workplace culture problems aren't hidden in the shadows, they're visible to a significant chunk of your workforce, which means trust is already compromised before you even notice the issue. The real problem isn't that bad stuff happens at work, it's that people are watching it happen and apparently not confident enough to report it through whatever channels you've built.

industry-news.title: 7 stories on the state of pay in the workplace
industry-news.excerpt: The standard 3% to 5% annual raise has lost its advantage, a recent analysis suggests.
industry-news.dwp_take: The old playbook of handing out 3-5% annual raises isn't cutting it anymore, and HR Dive dug into what's actually happening with compensation across different sectors. This matters because your best people are watching the market, and if your organization's raise strategy is stuck in 2015, you're going to lose them to competitors who get it. Here's the real talk: if you're still celebrating a 3% raise like it's a promotion, you're already behind, and your employees know it.

industry-news.title: Amid daunting constraints, companies say they remain committed to inclusion
industry-news.excerpt: However, federal contractors have faced regulatory pressure, prompting the majority to decrease inclusion efforts, per a report.
industry-news.dwp_take: Federal contractors are cutting their inclusion programs despite public commitments to diversity, thanks to regulatory pressure and legal uncertainty around DEI initiatives. This matters because digital workplace teams often own the platforms, communications, and collaboration tools that either enable or undermine inclusive hiring and employee experience, so budget cuts here hit your infrastructure plans too. The real story isn't the contradiction, it's that companies will abandon stated values the moment legal wind shifts, which should tell you something about how seriously to take their next "strategic initiative" announcement.

industry-news.title: Burnout is increasing, while employee confidence is at a record low, research shows
industry-news.excerpt: Worker burnout happens when employees “face a chronic, unmanageable amount” of stress, a senior economist for Glassdoor said.
industry-news.dwp_take: A new study shows burnout is climbing while employee confidence has hit the floor, which tracks with what we're all watching happen in real time. Digital workplace leaders need to stop treating this as an HR problem and start recognizing it as a technology and culture problem, because bad tools, poor communication systems, and always-on expectations are major burnout accelerators. The irony is that most organizations will respond by launching another wellness app instead of actually fixing the broken processes that are grinding people into dust.
